title: Insulation and Air Sealing Tips for a Cozier Home
h1: How Do Insulation and Air Sealing Make a Home More Comfortable?
description: How attic insulation and air sealing keep your home cooler in summer and warmer on cold nights, where the leaks hide, and what to fix first in a SoCal home.
quick_answer: Insulation slows heat moving through your ceilings and walls, and air sealing stops air from leaking in and out through gaps. Together they keep attic heat out in summer, hold warmth in on cold nights, and cut drafts and hot spots. In most San Diego and Orange County homes, the attic is the best place to start.
body:
What's the difference between insulation and air sealing?

They solve two different problems, and you usually need both.

  • Insulation slows heat moving through a surface, like heat from a hot attic coming down through your ceiling.
  • Air sealing closes the gaps and holes that let air itself move between your living space and the attic, walls or crawl space.

Insulation doesn't stop air very well. If warm air is leaking through an open gap around a light fixture, a thick layer of insulation on top of it won't fix the draft. That's why air sealing comes first and insulation goes on top.

Where does a typical SoCal home leak air?

Many homes here are older stucco tract houses with the furnace or air handler and ductwork in the attic. The common leak points are:

  • Recessed can lights and ceiling fixtures
  • The attic access hatch, which often has no seal or insulation
  • Plumbing vents and wiring holes drilled through the top plates of walls
  • Gaps around the furnace flue and bathroom fan housings
  • Leaky supply and return ducts in the attic
  • Gaps around windows, doors and the garage-to-house door

Crawl spaces matter too in homes that have them. Gaps around pipes and wiring in the floor let damp, musty crawl space air move up into the house, especially near the coast.

Each one is small, but together they can add up to a lot of open area, and they're often what makes one room feel very different from the rest of the house.

How do they make a home more comfortable?

On a summer afternoon, attic temperatures can climb well above the outdoor temperature, especially inland. Without good insulation, that heat radiates down through the ceiling and the rooms below stay warm well into the evening. Leaky ceilings let that hot attic air drift into the house too.

In winter, coastal days are mild but inland nights get cold. Warm air rises and escapes through ceiling gaps, pulling cold air in through gaps lower in the house. That's the drafty feeling near floors and windows.

Sealing and insulating the attic evens this out. Rooms stay closer to the thermostat setting, the system doesn't run as long to catch up, and upstairs bedrooms stop feeling like a different climate zone.

Does insulation help indoor air quality too?

Yes. Air that leaks in from the attic carries dust, insulation fibers and sometimes rodent debris. Sealing those leaks keeps that air out of your living space. Sealing leaky ducts in the attic matters for the same reason, since a leaky return duct pulls attic air right into the system.

If the existing insulation is matted, wet or contaminated by rodents, it should come out before new insulation goes in. Old, dirty insulation doesn't perform well and can hold odors and debris.

What should you do first?

  1. Get the attic inspected. Check the depth and condition of the insulation and look for signs of pests or moisture.
  2. Clean out damaged insulation if it's compressed, contaminated or wet.
  3. Air seal the attic floor around fixtures, penetrations and the access hatch.
  4. Seal and insulate ducts that run through the attic.
  5. Add insulation to the recommended depth, keeping it clear of soffit vents so the attic can still breathe.

How do you know if your attic needs work?

A few signs suggest your insulation or air sealing isn't doing its job:

  • Upstairs rooms or rooms under a flat ceiling are much hotter than the rest of the house in summer.
  • The AC runs for long stretches on warm afternoons and still can't keep up.
  • You can see the tops of the ceiling joists in the attic, which usually means the insulation is thin.
  • Insulation looks flattened, stained or has droppings in it.
  • Rooms feel drafty on cold inland nights even with windows closed.

Our attic insulation team handles cleanup, air sealing and new insulation as one job, so the work is done in the right order.
faqs: Can you add new insulation over old insulation?

Sometimes. If the old insulation is dry, clean and just thin, adding more on top can work. If it's compressed, wet, moldy or contaminated by rodents, it should be removed first. Topping off damaged insulation buries the problem and you won't get the full benefit of the new layer.
Should I air seal before adding insulation?

Yes. Once insulation is blown in, the gaps in the attic floor are buried and much harder to reach. Sealing first closes the air leaks, then insulation goes on top to slow heat flow. Doing it in that order gets the most comfort out of the work.
Will air sealing make my house too tight?

Most existing homes have plenty of leaks left even after attic sealing. Bathroom and kitchen exhaust fans still need to work, and combustion appliances need proper venting. A good contractor checks those details. If a home does end up very tight, a fresh air ventilator can bring in filtered outdoor air.
Does insulation matter in a mild climate like San Diego?

Yes. Attics get very hot in summer, especially inland, and that heat pushes down into your rooms. Inland nights also get cold in winter. Good insulation and air sealing keep rooms closer to the thermostat setting and help your HVAC system run less.
